summary: Describes how COPS should be used to provide policy services in RSVP environments. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2749 says how to use the COPS protocol with RSVP, the protocol that reserves network resources for a flow. A router asks a separate policy server whether a reservation is allowed, and the server answers with a decision that can approve, refuse, or adjust the request. The RFC defines which questions the router may ask, what the answer may contain, and the order in which the questions must be asked.

subtitle: How a router asks a policy server for permission to reserve network resources, and how the answer is used.

tldr.problem: A router that reserves resources for a flow has to decide whether the reservation is allowed, and that decision belongs to policy, not to the router. Without a common way to ask, each router would make its own choice.
tldr.mechanism: The router, a policy enforcement point, sends COPS requests to a policy decision point. Each request carries a context saying which step is involved, a message type, and the RSVP objects received. The policy server answers with a decision that can install or remove the request, add policy data, or replace objects in the message.
tldr.outcome: Policy decisions for RSVP can live on a server instead of in every router, while the router keeps the local decision point for the moments when it cannot reach the server. The RFC is a usage document on top of the COPS protocol and the RSVP specification.

today: RFC 2749 is a Proposed Standard from January 2000 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It is a usage document that sits on three others: RFC 2748 defines the COPS protocol it specialises, RFC 2750 the RSVP policy extensions it refers to, and RFC 2205 the RSVP specification whose objects it carries. The admission control framework it assumes is RFC 2753.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The Common Open Policy Service (COPS) is a query and response protocol used to exchange policy information between a network policy server and a set of clients. It is being developed within the RSVP Admission Policy Working Group of the IETF, primarily as a mechanism for providing policy-based admission control over requests for network resources.

This document gives usage directives for using COPS when RSVP clients outsource policy control decisions to policy servers. The client that enforces policy is the policy enforcement point (PEP), normally a router, and the server that makes the decision is the policy decision point (PDP). RSVP registers with COPS as client type 1.

Because COPS is already designed, the directives here are mainly about RSVP applicability, interoperability and usage guidelines, together with client specific examples. The document assumes prior knowledge of the RAP framework and of the basic COPS protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: COPS lets a router ask a policy server whether a request should be allowed and get back an answer. RFC 2749 says how to use that mechanism with RSVP, which reserves network resources for a flow. It defines the questions the router may ask, the answers a policy server may give, and the order in which the router must ask them.

sections.title: The Context Object
sections.content:
The Context object says what the PEP is asking about. It has two parts: an R-Type, the request type flag, which names the situation the question belongs to, and an M-Type, which identifies the applicable RSVP message type.

There are three request types. The Incoming-Message request is used when the PEP has received an RSVP message. The PDP may decide to accept or reject it and may also apply other decision objects to it; if the incoming message is rejected, RSVP should treat it as if it never arrived. The Resource-Allocation request is used when the PEP is about to commit local resources to an RSVP flow, so it applies to Resv messages only, and the decision is made for the merge of all reservations associated with the flow, which may have arrived on a particular interface from several RSVP next hops. The Outgoing-Message request is used when the PEP is about to forward an outgoing RSVP message; the PDP may allow or deny that message and may provide an outgoing policy data object.

The M-Type values are identical to the values used in the msg type field of the RSVP header. Four message types are supported: Path, Resv, PathErr and ResvErr. Other message types such as PathTear, ResvTear and Resv Confirm are not supported, and the list of supported types can only be extended in later versions of RSVP or of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Every question the router asks carries a context saying which step it is about: a message arriving, local resources being committed, or a message about to be forwarded. It also names the RSVP message type involved. Only Path, Resv, PathErr and ResvErr can be used.

sections.title: Client Specific Information
sections.content:
All the objects that were received in an RSVP message are encapsulated inside the Client Specific Information object, in the form called Signaled ClientSI, and sent from the PEP to the remote PDP. The PEP and the PDP share RSVP state, and the PDP is assumed to implement the same RSVP functional specification as the PEP.

If the PDP detects the absence of objects required by the RSVP specification, it should return an Error in the Decision message indicating that mandatory client-specific info is missing. If it detects the absence of optional RSVP objects that are needed to approve the request against current policies, it should return a negative Decision instead.

Unlike the Incoming and Outgoing contexts, Resource Allocation is not always directly associated with a specific RSVP message. In a multicast session it may represent the merging of multiple incoming reservations, so the ClientSI object should specifically contain the SESSION and STYLE objects along with the merged FLOWSPEC, the FILTERSPEC list, and the SCOPE object whenever relevant.
sections.plainLanguage: The router copies the RSVP objects it received into a client information object and sends that to the policy server, which is assumed to understand RSVP as well as the router does. For a merged multicast reservation, the object has to carry the merged flow specification, the filter list and the scope.

sections.title: The Decision Object
sections.content:
The Decision object is how the PDP controls the PEP. While accepting an RSVP message, a PDP may use decision commands, flags and objects to provide preemption priority, trigger warnings, replace RSVP objects and more.

Only two decision commands apply to RSVP. Install is the positive response: accept, allow or admit an RSVP message or a local resource allocation. Remove is the negative response: deny, reject or remove an RSVP message or a local resource allocation.

Only one decision flag applies to RSVP. When the Trigger Error flag is set, RSVP should schedule a PathErr in response to a Path message, or a ResvErr in response to a Resv message.

Stateless Policy Data may include one or more policy elements, as specified for the RSVP Policy Data object, which are assumed to be well understood by the client's local policy decision point. The PEP should consider these as an addition to the decision already received from the PDP, since it can add but cannot override. Stateless objects must be well understood but not necessarily supported by all PEPs, so the PDP must be prepared for them to be ignored.

Replacement Data may contain multiple RSVP objects to be replaced from the original RSVP request. Replacement is typically performed on the Forward Outgoing request, for instance replacing outgoing Policy Data, but it is not limited to that and can also be performed on other contexts such as Resource-Allocation. Replacing the RSVP FlowSpec object can be useful for controlling resources across a trusted zone of policy ignorant nodes. RSVP clients are currently only required to allow replacement of three objects, POLICY_DATA, ERROR_SPEC and FLOWSPEC, but could optionally support replacement of other objects.

Replacement works in a fixed way. If no Replacement Data decision appears in a decision message, all signaled objects are processed as if the PDP was not there. When an object of a certain C-Num appears, it replaces all the instances of that C-Num in the RSVP message, and if it appears empty, with a length of 4, it removes all the instances without adding anything.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy server answers with a Decision object. It can install or remove the request, ask RSVP to raise an error, add policy elements, or replace objects in the original message. Replacement is all or nothing for a given object type: a new object replaces every copy of it, and an empty one deletes every copy.

sections.title: Running COPS for RSVP Flows
sections.content:
Policy control is performed per RSVP flow, where a flow is the atomic unit of an RSVP reservation, a TC reservation. Reservation styles also affect the definition of a flow: a set of senders that is considered a single flow for a WF reservation is considered a set of individual flows when FF style is used. Several FF flows may be packed into a single Resv message, and a packed message must be unpacked so that a separate request is issued for each of the packed flows, as if they were individual RSVP messages. Each COPS request should include the associated POLICY_DATA objects, which by default are all the POLICY_DATA objects in the packed message.

When making a decision, the PDP may consider both the Resv and its matching Path state. State association is straightforward in the common unicast case, because the RSVP flow includes one Path state and one Resv state. In multicast cases the correspondence may be more complicated, as the match may be many-to-many, and the COPS protocol assumes that the PDP is RSVP knowledgeable and capable of determining these associations from the contents of the request and especially the ClientSI object.

Admission of a new reservation requires both an administrative approval, which is the policy control, and capacity admission control. After it has been approved by both, and after the reservation was successfully installed, the PEP notifies the remote PDP by sending a report message specifying the Commit type. That report signals when billing should effectively begin and when heavier delayed operations, such as debiting a credit card, are permissible. If a reservation approved by the PDP fails admission because of a lack of resources, the PEP must issue a no-commit report, fold back and send an updated request to its previous state, and, if no state was previously installed, issue a delete (DRQ).

PathTear and ResvTear messages are not controlled by this policy architecture. That relies on two assumptions: that MD5 authentication verifies the tear was received from the same node that sent the initial reservation, and that it is functionally equivalent to that node holding off refreshes for the reservation. When a ResvTear or PathTear is received at the PEP, all affected states installed on the PDP should either be deleted or updated by the PEP.

Because COPS is a stateful protocol, refreshes for RSVP Path and Resv messages need not be constantly sent to the remote PDP. Once a decision has been returned for a request, the PEP can cache that decision and apply it to future refreshes, and it should update the PDP with the new request state when it detects a change in the corresponding Resv or Path message. If the connection between the PEP and the PDP is lost, the cached RSVP state may be retained for the RSVP timeout period and used for previously admitted flows, but it cannot be applied to new or updated state. If the connection cannot be reestablished with the PDP or a backup PDP after that timeout, the PEP is expected to purge all its cached decisions; without an applicable cached decision it must either reject the flow or resort to its local policy decision point. Once a connection is reestablished to a new or the original PDP, the PDP may issue a state synchronization request, and the PEP must then reissue requests that correspond to the current RSVP state, as if all the state had just been updated.
sections.plainLanguage: The router asks about one flow at a time, and it can reuse the last answer for later refreshes of that flow until something changes or the connection to the policy server drops. It reports a commit only once the reservation is both approved and installed, so that billing starts at the right moment.

sections.title: RSVP Error Reporting
sections.content:
RSVP uses the ERROR_SPEC object in PathErr and ResvErr messages to report policy errors. While the contents of the ERROR_SPEC object are defined by the RSVP specification and its extensions, the PDP is in the best position to provide them, including the sub-codes.

The procedure is this. First the PEP queries the PDP before sending a PathErr or ResvErr, and then the PDP returns the constructed ERROR_SPEC in the Replacement Data decision object, so the error message carries the details the policy server chose.
sections.plainLanguage: When a policy error has to be reported, the router asks the policy server for the error details first, and then sends the error message to the sender.

sections.title: Unicast and Multicast Examples
sections.content:
The unicast example has a PEP router with two interfaces. A sender S1 sends to a receiver R1, and a Path message arrives from S1. The PEP sends a request whose context is in and out for the Path, giving the in interface and the out interface and all the objects in the Path message, and the PDP answers with an Install decision for both contexts.

A Resv message then arrives from R1. The PEP asks with a context of in, allocation and out, and the PDP answers with three separate decisions, one per context: Install for the incoming context, Install plus a stateless priority of 7 for the allocation context, and Install plus a replacement of POLICY-DATA1 for the outgoing context. The decision was split because different decision objects applied to different context flags. The PEP then reports a commit for that handle.

Later the PDP changes its decision and answers with Install plus a stateless priority of 3 for the allocation context. Because the priority is now too low, the PEP preempts the flow and sends a delete request with the reason code Preempted. When the sender stops sending Path messages, the PEP sends a delete for the Path handle with the reason Timeout.

The multicast example has a PEP with two senders and three receivers in one session, with if2 on a shared medium. A Path message arrives on if3 from S1 and is approved. The forwarding table then gives two outgoing interfaces for that path, so two separate exchanges are needed, one for if1 and one for if2. A WF Resv message from R2 on if2 is approved with a preemption priority of 5, and the PEP reports a commit.

When a second WF Resv with a higher RSpec arrives from R3 on the same interface, the PEP can no longer combine context flags, because two reservations arrived on that interface, so it issues the requests separately: the incoming context first, then the allocation context, which again returns a priority of 5 and a commit. If a ResvErr arrives from S1, the PEP maps it to R3 alone, because R3 has the higher flow specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the whole exchange for one reservation and for a shared multicast session. In both cases the router sends a request, the policy server answers with an install decision, and the router reports a commit once the reservation is in place.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document relies on COPS for its signalling and for its security, and refers the reader to the security considerations section of the COPS specification.

Security for RSVP messages is provided by inter-router MD5 authentication, assuming a chain-of-trust model. A likely deployment scenario calls for PEPs to be deployed only at the network edge, on boundary nodes, while the core of the network, the backbone, consists of policy ignorant nodes. In that scenario MD5 trust between boundary PEPs that are not neighbours is established through internal signing, that is integrity, of the Policy Data object itself, which is left unmodified as it passes through the policy ignorant nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: The security of the exchange comes from COPS and from MD5 authentication between routers, which is why the design keeps policy servers at the edge of the network and leaves the core routers policy ignorant.

items.title: Install
items.text: Positive response: accept, allow or admit an RSVP message or a local resource allocation.

items.title: Remove
items.text: Negative response: deny, reject or remove an RSVP message or a local resource allocation.

items.title: Trigger Error
items.text: The only decision flag for RSVP: schedule a PathErr for a Path message, or a ResvErr for a Resv message.

items.title: Stateless Policy Data
items.text: Policy elements the PEP may add to the decision, but never override.

items.title: Replacement Data
items.text: Objects that replace, or with a length of 4 remove, every instance of the same object in the RSVP message.

messages.label: REQ, context in and out, Path
messages.note: Handle A, in interface if2, out interface if1, all objects in the Path message.

messages.label: REQ, context in, allocation and out, Resv
messages.note: Handle B, in interface if1, out interface if2.

messages.label: DEC split by context
messages.note: Install for each context, stateless priority 7 on allocation, replacement POLICY-DATA1 on outgoing.

messages.label: RPT, commit
messages.note: The reservation was installed, so the PEP confirms the commit.
